knowledge_point.title: Reconstructing a Two-Variable Function From Its Gradient

question.:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $∇f=F,$ where $F(x,y)=(2 y)\,i+(2 x - 6)\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2 y,\qquad \frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x - 6.
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x\\&=\int (2 y)\,\text{d}x\\&=2 x y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x+g'(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x - 6$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x+g'(y)&=2 x - 6\\g'(y)&=-6\\g(y)&=- 6 y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=- 6 y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=2 x y - 6 y+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $∇f=F,$ where $F(x,y)=(4 x \sin{\left(y \right)})\,i+(2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 y^{2})\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4 x \sin{\left(y \right)},\qquad \frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 y^{2}.
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x\\&=\int (4 x \sin{\left(y \right)})\,\text{d}x\\&=2 x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)}+g'(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 y^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)}+g'(y)&=2 x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 y^{2}\\g'(y)&=6 y^{2}\\g(y)&=2 y^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=2 y^{3}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=2 x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} + 2 y^{3}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $∇f=F,$ where $F(x,y)=(2 y + 2 \sin{\left(y \right)})\,i+(2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x)\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2 y + 2 \sin{\left(y \right)},\qquad \frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x.
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x\\&=\int (2 y + 2 \sin{\left(y \right)})\,\text{d}x\\&=2 x y + 2 x \sin{\left(y \right)}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x+g'(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x+g'(y)&=2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 2 x\\g'(y)&=0\\g(y)&=0+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=0+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=2 x y + 2 x \sin{\left(y \right)}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $∇f=F,$ where $F(x,y)=(- 12 x^{2} + 4 y^{2})\,i+(8 x y - 16)\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=- 12 x^{2} + 4 y^{2},\qquad \frac{∂f}{∂y}=8 x y - 16.
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x\\&=\int (- 12 x^{2} + 4 y^{2})\,\text{d}x\\&=- 4 x^{3} + 4 x y^{2}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8 x y+g'(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8 x y - 16$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}8 x y+g'(y)&=8 x y - 16\\g'(y)&=-16\\g(y)&=- 16 y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=- 16 y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=- 4 x^{3} + 4 x y^{2} - 16 y+C.
$$
